The Watchmen That Went About the City Found Me
thuh WOCH-mun that WENT uh-BOWT thuh SIT-ee FOWND mee
n. phr. (the bride's second search in the Song, 5:7)
Hebrew m'tsā'ūnī hashshōm'rīm hassōb'bīm bā'īr — shāmar, to keep or guard, hence the watchmen; sābab, to go round, of their circuit of the walls.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The clause occurs twice and the second time is harder than the first. In Song 3:3 the bride, seeking him whom her soul loveth, meets the watchmen going about the city and asks them simply, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth? In 5:7, after she has been slow to open to her beloved and he has withdrawn, she goes out again and the same men treat her very differently: The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me. The men appointed to guard the city mistake the one person in it who has most right to be out, and the search that cost her nothing the first time costs her blood the second. Taken at the plain level the Song is Solomon's celebration of married love, and this is the night a wife's delay turns into a frightening search. Taken in the figure the church has long seen in the book, the passage is a severe and useful one: the soul that has been slow to open to Christ may find, when it rouses itself at last to seek Him, that He is not immediately found and that even the appointed keepers of the walls wound rather than help. She is not abandoned — the chapter ends with the great description of her Beloved — but she is not spared either.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Watchman, one set to guard a city and prevent danger. Veil, a cover; a curtain; a part of female dress. Song of Solomon 5:7, the keepers who wounded the seeker.

expand to see more

Watchman, a sentinel; one set to guard a city or camp and give notice of danger.

Keeper, one who holds or has possession; one who guards or preserves.

Veil, a cover; a curtain; a part of female dress which covers the face.

Hebrew shāmar, to keep, guard, watch over.

Hebrew sābab, to turn about, go round, make a circuit. Song 5:7.

Key Scripture

Son 3:3 — "The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?"

Son 5:6 — "I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer."

Son 5:7 — "The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me."

Son 5:8 — "I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love."

Modern Corruption

The passage is softened into a bad dream with no meaning, or it is read as proof that the church's officers are simply enemies of the devout soul.

expand to see more

Many expositors dispose of the scene by calling it a dream and leaving it there. The Song does say I sleep, but my heart waketh, and the dream framing is real; it is not an exemption from meaning. Scripture's dreams carry freight, and this one is placed with care immediately after a refusal: he knocked, she had put off her coat and would not rise, and by the time she opened he had withdrawn himself. The scene that follows is the cost of the delay, and softening it empties the warning the Song means to give.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a restraint in applying the figure. It is tempting, and now common, to read the watchmen simply as the institutional church and the beating as proof that the fervent soul should expect only harm from pastors and elders. The same book gives watchmen their honourable sense, Isaiah sets watchmen upon the walls who shall never hold their peace, and the New Testament commands obedience to those who watch for souls. What the passage teaches is that keepers can fail, and fail most when they are needed; not that keeping is the enemy. The bride does not renounce the city. She charges its daughters to tell her Beloved that she is sick of love.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shāmar, to guard, with sābab, to make a circuit — the city's own keepers wounding the bride on her second and costlier search.

expand to see more

Hebrew shāmar, to keep or guard; the participle gives watchmen.

Hebrew sābab, to go round about — their circuit of the walls.

Hebrew r'dīd, a wide wrapper or veil, taken from her.

The first meeting cost her nothing, Song 3:3; the second drew blood.

The scene follows her refusal to open, Song 5:3 and 5:6.

Usage

"the watchmen that went about the city found me"

"they smote me, they wounded me"

"I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself"
